warmup.q: A cron job runs rm /var/log/ledger/app.log to free space, while the payment service still has the file open and keeps logging to it. What happens to the disk space?
options: It's free at once: the file is gone
It stays in use until the service closes the file, though ls and du no longer show it
The service's next write fails with ENOENT and it stops logging
The kernel creates a new app.log at the service's next write
warmup.why: rm removes a name. The kernel frees the file's inode and blocks only when it has no names left and no process has it open. The service's file descriptor still points at it, so its writes keep landing in a file nobody can see by name, and df keeps counting it. The service gets no error, and nothing recreates the name.

sections.h: A file is an inode, and a name only points to it
sections.html:
stat on a file in the lab box prints Inode: 1573046 and Links: 1. Give the file a second name with ln, and stat on either name prints the same inode number and Links: 2. Two names, one file. To see why file systems work like that, start with what one has to store.

A disk is a long array of blocks, 4 KB each in this track. For every file, something must record which blocks hold its bytes, how many bytes there are, who owns it, who may read it and when it last changed. The simplest design keeps all of that next to the name, one row per file: name, owner, size, blocks. A directory would be a table of such rows.

It breaks on the first file you want under two names. The settlement job writes ledger.csv, and the audit export wants the same 2 GB file as ledger-2026.csv without copying it. With the size and block list stored next to each name, the two rows must agree forever. Append a record through one name and the other row's size is wrong.

So Unix splits the row in two. The inode (index node) is the file itself: its type, size, owner, permissions, timestamps, a link count and the list of blocks that hold the data. It has a number and no name. A directory is a file whose content is a list of entries, each one a name and an inode number. Opening /tmp/ledger.csv means reading the root directory to find tmp and its inode number, reading that directory to find ledger.csv and its number, then reading that inode.

A second name is just a second entry with the same number. That's a hard link, and the link count says how many entries point at the inode. rm doesn't delete a file. It calls unlink, which removes one entry and subtracts one from the count. The kernel frees the inode and its blocks when the count reaches 0 and, as section 3 shows, no process still has the file open. Renaming changes one entry and leaves the inode alone, which is why lesson 9 of this track could use rename to swap a file in one step.

A symbolic link works differently. It's an inode of its own whose content is a path: latest.csv holds the 10 bytes ledger.csv, and the kernel looks that path up again every time the link is opened. Remove the name it points to and the symlink dangles, while a hard link keeps working. A hard link holds only a number, so it can't reach into another file system, whose inode numbers mean something else, and Linux refuses hard links to directories, which could make loops in the tree.

try.title: Two names, one inode
steps: From the labs folder, start the lab box: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box.
The block makes a file, a hard link and a symlink, prints their inodes and link counts, then removes the original name. Predict what each cat prints and the link count after rm.
The last line traces the system calls behind ln, ln -s, mv and rm.

The hard link has the same inode as the original, and the count is 2. The symlink has its own inode and is 10 bytes long: the path ledger.csv. After rm, the data is still there through ledger-2026.csv, whose count dropped to 1, and the symlink fails because the name it holds is gone (cat's complaint prints last because it goes to standard error). The trace shows the four calls: linkat adds an entry for an existing inode, symlinkat makes a new inode holding a path, renameat2 moves an entry and unlinkat removes one. None of them touches the file's data.

sections.h: Three tables sit between a file descriptor and the inode
sections.html:
share.c lets a child process write three records to auth.log, then lets its parent write three more. Run one way, the file ends with all six records. Run another way, with exactly the same writes, it ends with the parent's three, and the child's are gone. The difference is where the file offset lives.

A file descriptor is the small number open() returns (lesson 1 of this track): 3 for the first file a program opens, because 0, 1 and 2 are standard input, output and error. Every read and write through it moves an offset, the position where the next byte goes. The obvious design keeps the offset in the descriptor: each process has its own fd numbers, and each fd has its own offset.

That design breaks shell redirection. (date; hostname) > out.txt runs two programs one after the other. The shell opened out.txt once, and both programs inherited fd 1 through fork and exec (lesson 2 of this track). If each had its own offset starting at 0, hostname would write over the output of date. In fact you get both lines, one under the other.

So Linux keeps three tables. Each process has an fd table that maps fd numbers to pointers. Each pointer leads to an open file description, made by one open() call, which holds the offset and the flags the file was opened with. The description points at the inode. fork copies the fd table, so the child's fd 3 reaches the parent's description, and the two share one offset. dup2, which a shell uses for >, does the same inside one process. A second open() of the same file, even by the same process, makes a new description with its own offset at 0. /proc/<pid>/fdinfo/<fd> prints the description's pos and flags.

That explains share.c. Opened once before fork, the child's writes move the shared offset to 42, the parent writes from 42, and nothing is lost. Opened separately after fork, the parent's description is still at 0, and its writes land on the child's bytes. The stepper walks through both.

Two processes that open one log file on their own, such as two JVMs or a service and a sidecar, need O_APPEND. With it, the kernel moves the offset to the end of the file before every write, in the same step as the write, so no writer lands on another's bytes. Java's FileOutputStream(file, true) opens a file this way, and so do Logback's and Log4j's file appenders by default. Keep one record per write() call as well: on Linux's local file systems another writer can't split a single write, but it can land between two.

sections.h: A deleted file lives until its last descriptor closes
sections.html:
LogHolder is a JVM that writes 40 MB to /dev/shm/auth.log and keeps logging into it. Delete the file under it, and df still says 41 MB of /dev/shm are in use, while du says 0.

Both are right. du walks directory entries and adds up the files they reach, and no entry reaches this inode any more. df asks the file system how many blocks are allocated, and these blocks still are. The rule from the first section has a second half: the kernel frees an inode when its link count is 0 and no open file description points at it. The JVM's fd 4 still points at a description, which still points at the inode, so the service keeps writing to a file nobody can find by name.

You can find it from the process's side. /proc/<pid>/fd/ has one entry per descriptor, and for a file that has lost every name it shows the old path followed by (deleted). lsof +L1 lists every open file with fewer than one link, which is exactly this case. The /proc entry also opens the file: cp /proc/<pid>/fd/4 recovered.log copies all 40 MB back out, for as long as the process lives.

On a server this shows up as a full disk nobody can explain. A cleanup job deletes old logs, or someone runs rm on a 20 GB log to make room, and the space doesn't come back until the service restarts. Two fixes don't need a restart. Truncate the file instead of deleting it, through its name (: > app.log) or, once it's deleted, through /proc (: > /proc/<pid>/fd/4), and df drops at once. That works cleanly when the writer opened the file with O_APPEND, because its next write goes to the new end. A writer without O_APPEND keeps its old offset, 40 MB in, and its next write leaves a 40 MB hole of zeros in front of it. The lasting fix is in how logs rotate. Let the logging framework roll its own files (Logback's and Log4j's rolling appenders rename the old file and open a new one), or, for a program that can't reopen its log, use logrotate's copytruncate, which copies the file and then truncates it in place.

The same rule works for you on purpose. A program can create a temporary file, open it and unlink it at once. Nobody else can open it by name, and the kernel frees it the moment the program closes it, even if the program crashes.

sections.h: Every open file and socket is a descriptor, and the table has a limit
sections.html:
FdLeak opens a config file for every "request" and never closes it. With the limit set to 256 descriptors, open number 253 fails with java.io.FileNotFoundException: /etc/hostname (Too many open files). The JVM already had 4 open (0, 1, 2 and the JDK's lib/modules file), and 4 + 252 is 256.

An fd table can't grow forever, because every entry pins kernel memory: the description and, behind it, a file, a socket's buffers or a pipe. So the kernel caps the table with a resource limit, RLIMIT_NOFILE, which ulimit -n sets. When a process holds as many descriptors as its limit, open, socket, accept and pipe all fail with EMFILE, which Java reports as "Too many open files". The name misleads: every TCP connection is a descriptor too, so a JDBC pool of 20 Oracle connections holds 20, an HTTP client keeping 200 connections alive holds 200, and a server holds one per client.

The limit has two values. The soft limit is the one the kernel enforces. A process may raise it up to the hard limit, and only a privileged process can raise the hard one. The JVM raises it for you: at start-up HotSpot sets the soft limit to the hard limit (the MaxFDLimit flag, on by default). strace shows the two calls, and a JVM started under ulimit -S -n 256 opened 5,000 files without trouble. So what limits a JVM is the hard limit: 1,048,576 in the lab box, Docker's default here. For a running service, grep 'open files' /proc/<pid>/limits tells you.

A high limit doesn't fix a leak. It only moves the failure. Above every process sits a limit for the whole machine, fs.file-max, 812,037 in this Docker VM. My first version of FdLeak had no cap. It reached that limit after 810,087 opens and failed with "Too many open files in system" (ENFILE), and for that moment every other process in the VM was refused new files too. FdLeak now stops itself at 5,000.

To watch a service, count its descriptors over time with ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l, or export the same number as a metric (Micrometer's process.files.open). A count that climbs with traffic and never comes back down is a leak: a stream, a socket or a Files.list result that nobody closes. In Java, try (...) closes it for you, and in Kotlin, use {}.

[pid    82] prlimit64(0, RLIMIT_NOFILE, NULL, {rlim_cur=256, rlim_max=1024*1024}) = 0
[pid    82] prlimit64(0, RLIMIT_NOFILE, {rlim_cur=1024*1024, rlim_max=1024*1024}, NULL) = 0
106   openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/hostname", O_RDONLY) = -1 EMFILE (Too many open files)

The soft limit alone stops nothing: the JVM reads {rlim_cur=256, rlim_max=1024*1024} and sets the soft limit to the hard one before your code runs, so all 5,000 opens work. With the hard limit at 256 too, the 253rd open fails, the kernel returns EMFILE and Java throws. The JVM started with 4 descriptors, so the table was full at exactly 256.

sections.h: A journal keeps inodes and blocks consistent through a crash
sections.html:
debugfs reads an ext4 file system straight from its disk image. For ledger.csv it prints Inode: 13, Size: 31, Links: 2 and, under EXTENTS, (0):2065: block 0 of the file is block 2065 of the disk. That's the inode from the first section, as bytes on a disk.

Adding one block to a file changes at least three places on the disk: the new data block, the block bitmap (one bit per block, set while the block is in use) and the inode (a new size and a new extent). The disk writes them one at a time. Lose power between two of those writes, and the file system contradicts itself. A block marked as used that no inode owns is lost space. An inode pointing at a block that the bitmap still calls free is worse: the next file gets that block too, and two files share bytes.

The old fix was fsck. After every crash, it reads every inode and every bitmap and repairs what disagrees. On a big disk that takes minutes to hours, and the server can't start until it's done.

A journal turns the scattered writes into one decision. The file system first writes every changed block to a log area of its own (inode 8, 4 MB in the Try-it's image), then a commit record. Only after the commit is on disk does it copy those blocks to their real places, a step called checkpointing. After a crash, the mount replays each transaction that has a commit record and ignores the one that doesn't, in about the time it takes to read the journal. The figure shows the order.

ext4 by default journals metadata only (inodes, bitmaps, directories) in the mode data=ordered. Its documentation puts it this way: "All data are forced directly out to the main file system prior to its metadata being committed to the journal." So after a crash, an inode never points at a block that still holds some other file's old bytes. ext4 commits a transaction at least every 5 seconds (commit=5). XFS has the same shape at this level: it logs metadata changes, not file data, and it splits the disk into allocation groups so many threads can allocate space at once.

Keep lesson 9's rule next to this one. A journal makes the file system's structure survive a crash, and nothing more. Data you wrote without fsync can still be missing afterwards, and a file can come back shorter than your last write() left it.

try.title: Read an inode and the journal off a disk image
steps: This one needs the privileged box, because it mounts a disk image: from the labs folder, docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box-priv.

OSTEP chapter 42: Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling

analogy: Think of the inode as an object on the JVM heap and a directory as a Map<String, Inode>. A hard link is a second map entry referring to the same object, and rm removes an entry, not the object. An open file description is an iterator over the object, with its own position: fork hands the same iterator to the child, while a second open() makes a new iterator at position 0. The object goes away when no map entry and no iterator refers to it. The analogy breaks on how that's decided. The JVM's garbage collector traces from roots and handles cycles. The kernel counts: a link count plus a count of open descriptions, freed the moment both are zero. Counting can't free a cycle, and that's one reason Linux won't let you hard-link a directory.
world: Payment services trip over this lesson in two ways. The first is a disk that fills up although the files are gone: a cleanup job or a person deleted a large log while the JVM still held it, and on Kubernetes a node under disk pressure may even evict pods for it. lsof +L1 on the node, or /proc/<pid>/fd in the container, shows the culprit, and truncating through /proc frees it without a restart. The second is "Too many open files", which is almost never about files. Every Oracle connection in a HikariCP pool, every Kafka broker connection, every keep-alive connection an HTTP client holds to the card issuer is a descriptor. A leak, such as a Files.list stream in a health check or a Response body nobody closes, grows the count with traffic until the next connection attempt fails. Export process.files.open next to process.files.max and alert on the ratio, not on the error.
mistake: Deleting a log file to free disk space while the service that writes it is still running. It feels like the direct fix: the file is big, remove it. The space doesn't come back, because rm only removes the name and the service's open descriptor keeps the inode and its blocks alive. People then delete more files, or restart the service at a bad time, without knowing why the first delete did nothing. Truncate instead (: > app.log, or truncate -s 0 app.log), which frees the blocks at once and keeps the writer's descriptor valid. If the file is already deleted, find it with lsof +L1 and truncate it through /proc/<pid>/fd/<n>. For the long term, let the logging framework roll its own files, or configure logrotate with copytruncate for programs that can't reopen their logs.

compare.title: Open before fork against open after fork

a.label: open, then fork
a.title: one description: the file gets 84 bytes, all six records
a.html: int fd = open("auth.log", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644); if (fork() == 0) { // the child's fd 3 points at the SAME description records(fd, "child"); // shared offset: 0 -> 42 _exit(0); } wait(NULL); records(fd, "parent"); // starts at 42: 42 -> 84 // child auth 1 ... child auth 3 // parent auth 1 ... parent auth 3

b.label: fork, then open
b.title: two descriptions: 42 bytes, the child's records are gone
b.html: if (fork() == 0) { int fd = open("auth.log", O_WRONLY); // the child's own description records(fd, "child"); // its offset: 0 -> 42 _exit(0); } int fd = open("auth.log", O_WRONLY); // the parent's own, at 0 wait(NULL); records(fd, "parent"); // writes over bytes 0 to 42 // parent auth 1 ... parent auth 3

compare.note: The writes are the same on both sides; only the number of open() calls differs. One open makes one open file description, and fork shares it, offset included. Two open calls make two descriptions, each starting at 0, and the later writer wins. Adding O_APPEND to the opens on the right gives the left side's result, because the kernel then moves each description to the end of the file before every write.

worked.title: Find what holds a deleted file and free the space

steps.say: Start from the symptom. A volume is full, and du over it adds up to far less than df says is used. The gap is blocks that no name reaches. Here it's the whole 41 MB.
steps.code: df -m /dev/shm # Filesystem 1M-blocks Used Available Use% Mounted on # shm 64 41 24 63% /dev/shm du -sm /dev/shm # 0 /dev/shm

steps.say: Find the holder. lsof +L1 lists open files with a link count below 1. Without lsof, search the fd entries of every process for (deleted).
steps.code: lsof +L1 # COMMAND PID USER FD TYPE DEVICE SIZE/OFF NLINK NODE NAME # java 33 root 4w REG 0,179 41943200 0 2 /dev/shm/auth.log (deleted) find /proc/[0-9]*/fd -lname '*(deleted)' 2>/dev/null # /proc/33/fd/4

steps.say: Check how the file was opened before you truncate it. In fdinfo, the flags are octal: 01 is O_WRONLY and 02000 is O_APPEND. With O_APPEND, the writer's next line goes to the new end; without it, it lands at the old offset and leaves a hole.
steps.code: grep -E 'pos|flags' /proc/33/fdinfo/4 # pos: 41943348 # flags: 0402001

steps.say: Keep a copy if you need the contents, then truncate through /proc. The blocks are freed at once, and the service keeps running and logging.
steps.code: cp /proc/33/fd/4 /tmp/recovered.log : > /proc/33/fd/4 df -m /dev/shm # shm 64 0 64 0% /dev/shm

steps.say: Then fix the cause: whatever deleted the file should truncate or rename it instead, and the service should open a new file when its log rolls.

lab.title: Build a file system with inodes, links and shared offsets
steps: Read FileSystem.kt. Inode, OpenFile (the open file description) and Proc (a process's fd table) are the three tables. Path lookup, mkdir, symlink, rename, read, dup2, exit, dfBlocks and duBlocks are written for you, and so are the private helpers you'll call: parent (the directory and last name of a path), newInode, desc (the description behind an fd), release and dropName.
Run the tests from the labs folder. All eleven fail.
Write link and unlink. A name is an entry in a directory's entries map; the inode keeps the count in links.

Write open and close. open refuses with EMFILE at the limit, creates the file with CREATE, makes a new OpenFile and takes the lowest free fd. close frees the description on its last reference, and then maybe the inode.
Write write and fork. The three share.c tests replay the C program's three runs against its captured output, offsets included.
hints: fork must put the same OpenFile object in the child's table and add one to its refs. A copy of the object would give the child its own offset, which is what open does.
In write, handle APPEND first: set the offset to data.length, then write. StringBuilder.replace(start, end, text) overwrites from start and grows the builder when the text runs past the end.
Only decrement inode.openFiles when a description's refs reaches 0, then call release. That's what keeps a deleted file alive while any process holds it.
The lowest free fd: start at 0 and count up while fd in p.fds.

drill.title: Draw the tables after a fork and a second open
drill.prompt: A process opens ledger.csv (fd 3), forks, and then the child opens ledger.csv again (fd 4). The child writes 10 bytes to fd 3 and 5 bytes to fd 4; then the parent writes 7 bytes to fd 3. None of the opens used O_APPEND. From memory, write down how many open file descriptions exist, which fds point at each, each description's offset at the end, and the file's size.

answer.html:
descriptions: 2
  D1 (the parent's open, before fork): parent fd 3, child fd 3   refs 2
  D2 (the child's second open):       child fd 4                 refs 1

child writes 10 bytes on fd 3  -> D1 offset 0 -> 10
child writes  5 bytes on fd 4  -> D2 offset 0 -> 5   (over bytes 0-4)
parent writes 7 bytes on fd 3  -> D1 offset 10 -> 17

end: D1 offset 17, D2 offset 5, file size 17
one inode, link count 1, open descriptions 2

recap: An inode is the file: type, size, owner, permissions, times, link count and block list, but no name. A directory maps names to inode numbers.
A hard link is another name for the same inode; a symlink is its own inode holding a path. rm is unlink: one name less, and the inode is freed when no names and no open descriptions remain.
Three tables: the per-process fd table points at open file descriptions (offset and flags, one per open()), which point at inodes. fork and dup2 share descriptions; a second open() makes a new one.
O_APPEND moves the offset to the end before every write, so separate writers don't overwrite each other.
A deleted file that's still open keeps its space: df counts it, du doesn't. Find it with lsof +L1 or /proc/<pid>/fd, and truncate it to free the space.

Sockets count as descriptors too. The JVM raises its soft RLIMIT_NOFILE to the hard limit; a leak ends in EMFILE, or ENFILE at the machine's fs.file-max. A journal keeps metadata consistent through a crash, not your un-fsynced data.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why the settlement service's disk was still full after they deleted its 20 GB log, and why it only cleared after a restart. Explain it, and say what they should do next time.
explain.answer: A file on Linux is an inode, and its name is just an entry in a directory pointing at that inode. rm removes the entry and lowers the link count to 0, but the kernel only frees the inode and its blocks when no process has the file open either. The service still had the log open, through a file descriptor that points at an open file description, which points at the inode. So the 20 GB stayed allocated, the service kept writing into a file nobody could see by name, and df and du disagreed. The restart closed the descriptor, and that's when the space came back. Next time, truncate the file instead of deleting it, with : > app.log, which frees the blocks at once and leaves the service's descriptor working. If it's already deleted, lsof +L1 shows which process holds it, and truncating /proc/<pid>/fd/<n> frees it without a restart. Because our logger opens with O_APPEND, its next line simply goes to the start of the empty file. And whatever cleans up logs should rename or truncate them, so the logging framework can roll to a new file.

deeper.html:
A file system can run out of inodes before it runs out of space. ext4 makes a fixed number when you run mkfs (16,384 for the 64 MB image in the last Try-it, one per 4 KB block in a small image). A volume full of tiny files, such as a mail spool or a cache that writes one file per key, can show free blocks in df -h and still refuse new files with ENOSPC. df -i shows inode use. XFS allocates inodes as it needs them, so it rarely hits this.

Small files have their own tricks. The symlink in the Try-it had Blockcount: 0: ext4 stores a target shorter than 60 bytes inside the inode itself (a "fast symlink"). And a file can have holes. Writing at offset 1 GB in an empty file makes its size 1 GB, but blocks are allocated only where data was written; ls -l shows the size and du shows the blocks. That's the hole a writer without O_APPEND leaves after you truncate its file under it.

Linux has a direct way to make a file that never has a name: open(dir, O_TMPFILE | O_RDWR) creates an unnamed inode in that directory's file system. You can write it, fsync it, and if you decide to keep it, give it a name with linkat from /proc/self/fd/<n>. It's another way to publish a complete file in one step, next to the temp-file-and-rename pattern from lesson 9.

For ext4's journal itself, /proc/fs/jbd2/<device>/info prints how many transactions committed and how long they took, and the mount option data=journal puts file data through the journal too: every block is written twice, and a small file is fully consistent after a crash. Almost nobody runs it, because the double writes cost throughput.
